tldr: Instead of collecting real-world data with expensive, fragile multi-fingered hands, this study gathers 75 hours of teleoperation demonstrations inside a VR simulation to pre-train a policy, achieving complex real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation with just 1–2 hours of physical fine-tuning.
hero_caption: Overall flow of Simulation Pre-training for Dexterity (SPD). Top: Operators use VR headsets to collect 75 hours of diverse bimanual dexterous manipulation data entirely inside a simulator. Bottom: The pre-trained model is fine-tuned with roughly 1 hour of physical demonstrations, enabling autonomous execution of complex real-world contact-rich tasks.
overview:
In recent years, pre-training robot policies on large-scale datasets has shown impressive results, but most of this progress has centered on simple parallel-jaw grippers. Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands has lagged behind because real hardware is expensive and prone to breaking, making it extremely difficult to collect long hours of teleoperation data. Meanwhile, using human hand video faces major hurdles: hand occlusions lead to inaccurate pose estimation, and structural differences create a significant embodiment gap.

To solve this, the authors asked: could we teleoperate robot hands directly inside a physics simulator using VR to gather large amounts of data safely, without physical hardware? In the proposed framework, Simulation Pre-training for Dexterity (SPD), human operators use a VR headset to control the target robot directly within a virtual environment across diverse contact-rich tasks. In simulation, resetting object placements takes an instant, and data collection can scale in parallel without worrying about hardware damage.

With five operators, the authors collected 75 hours of bimanual dexterous manipulation data over one week and pre-trained a Diffusion Transformer policy. They then fine-tuned the model on a real-world 56-DoF bimanual dexterous setup using only 1–2 hours of physical demonstrations per task.

As a result, across five physical tasks—plate racking, mug hanging, playing Jenga, cup stacking, and throwing bottles into a bin—SPD significantly outperformed behavior cloning baselines trained from scratch on real data alone. Furthermore, the experiments revealed that conditioning on past observation history enables fast replanning with short action chunks, unlocking the maximum benefits of simulation pre-training.
contributions: Developed "spd-vr", a VR simulation environment for low-cost, robot-free teleoperation data collection of multi-fingered hands.
Built and released "spd-75h", a large-scale bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset comprising 75 hours (1,930 episodes) across 6 diverse scenes and hundreds of virtual objects.
Demonstrated that policies pre-trained on simulation data clearly outperform imitation learning from scratch after only 1–2 hours of real-world fine-tuning.
Showed via ablation studies that combining observation history with short action chunks is essential for balancing reactivity and temporal consistency in contact-rich multi-fingered control.

sections.heading: Why Simulation Works for Pre-training Dexterous Hands
sections.summary: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands involves high contact and partial observability, making large-scale real-world data collection difficult due to costs and hardware failure risks. This paper presents SPD, which collects 75 hours of demonstrations directly via VR teleoperation in simulation and fine-tunes policies on physical hardware.
sections.details:
Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is full of contacts and severe occlusions caused by hands and objects, demanding millisecond-level control. Behavior cloning is an effective approach, but achieving sufficient performance requires massive and diverse demonstration datasets.

Recently, the paradigm of pre-training visuomotor representations on large-scale multi-task data and fine-tuning on a small target dataset has achieved great success. However, teleoperating real hardware is expensive. Multi-fingered hands are especially delicate and prone to breaking, which bottlenecks long-term collection throughput. On the other hand, learning from human video provides abundant data, but complex finger contacts and occlusions make accurate pose estimation difficult, introducing retargeting gaps in contact points and joint actuation.

This study focuses on VR teleoperation directly inside a physics simulator. The proposed framework, Simulation Pre-training for Dexterity (SPD), aligns the pre-training VR system ("spd-vr") and the physical teleoperation system ("spd-teleop") with identical robot configurations: dual arms, two 22-DoF hands, and cameras on the head and both wrists.

The main benefit of simulation is complete independence from physical hardware. If an attempt fails, virtual objects can be reset instantly with a single keystroke, making distributed, parallel data collection across multiple operators straightforward. Using five operators, the authors collected 75 hours of bimanual dexterous manipulation data across 6 scenes and hundreds of objects in just one week. Fine-tuning this pre-trained policy on physical tasks yields much greater robustness than training from scratch.

sections.heading: From Parallel Grippers to Multi-Fingered Hands, and Videos to Simulation
sections.summary: Existing large-scale robot pre-training has focused primarily on parallel-jaw grippers, while human video approaches suffer from embodiment gaps. This work introduces a new direction by using simulation teleoperation to collect target-embodiment, action-labeled data at scale without lossy retargeting.
sections.details:
Pre-training robot policies has rapidly evolved through multi-task imitation learning and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, most existing large datasets and models, such as ALOHA, are built for simple two-finger parallel-jaw grippers. Whether the same scaling laws hold for high-dimensional, contact-rich multi-fingered hands has remained an open question.

To lower the cost of real-world data collection, handheld interfaces without full robot bodies (such as UMI) and pre-training from human videos have been widely studied. Yet scaling handheld tools to high-DoF hands is mechanically challenging, and video-based learning lacks action labels, forcing reliance on latent action estimation or imperfect pose estimation. Wearable devices like exoskeleton gloves also tend to restrict natural, fine-grained finger movements.

In the multi-fingered hand domain, Sim-to-Real transfer using physics simulation and reinforcement learning (RL) has a long history. However, most prior works targeted a single specific skill, such as solving a Rubik's cube.

SPD takes a decisively different stance by treating simulation as a source of large-scale pre-training data for general-purpose visuomotor policies. By collecting action-labeled data directly on the target hand embodiment from the start, it avoids unnatural retargeting from humans to robots and learns foundational representations that transfer well across diverse tasks.

sections.heading: VR Teleoperation System and Causal Diffusion Transformer
sections.summary: Diverse, contact-rich behaviors were collected in the "spd-vr" simulation, matching the hardware and camera setup of the physical "spd-teleop" system. The policy is a causal Diffusion Transformer that generates future action chunks via flow matching conditioned on past visuomotor history.
sections.details:
The system consists of data collection platforms (simulation and real-world) and a policy architecture.

### 3.1 VR Data Collection (spd-vr)
Running in the MuJoCo physics simulator, operator wrist poses and finger positions estimated by Meta Quest 3 cameras are mapped in real time to a virtual bimanual dexterous robot using inverse kinematics (IK) (simulation at 480 Hz, control and streaming at 60 Hz). Six scenes were prepared: word blocks, dishes, mugs, bottles, cups, and Jenga. Physical properties and initial object poses were randomized each episode. Tasks were designed to be open-ended without rigid procedural steps, allowing diverse grasping strategies and behaviors to emerge naturally across operators (Figure F2).
After collection, idle periods without contacts were automatically trimmed, and images were rendered in parallel using the Madrona engine. GPU-based data augmentations, including texture replacement and left-right symmetry flipping (mirroring arms and camera views), were applied.

### 3.2 Real-World Data Collection (spd-teleop)
Physical hardware consists of two YAM Pro arms with reinforced gear ratios and two 22-DoF Sharpa Wave hands (56 DoF total). Three RealSense D405 cameras (one head-mounted, two on the wrists) match the exact geometry of the VR environment. Real-world teleoperation uses Manus data gloves, which resist visual occlusions, paired with Quest controllers for millimeter-precise control.

### 3.3 Policy Architecture and Training
To model diverse multimodal action distributions, the authors adopted a Diffusion Transformer based on Flow Matching (222M parameters). Instead of natural language instructions, the policy conditions on past visuomotor history (Figure F3).
Images from each camera are encoded by a pre-trained ViT and compressed into compact token sequences via cross-attention with learnable queries. The model receives proprioception (joint states), past actions, image tokens, and noisy action chunks as an interleaved sequence. By applying a causal mask, all chunks in a sequence are denoised in parallel during training for computational efficiency. During inference, sliding window attention with a window size of 32 steps is used, allowing the KV cache to remain fixed in length.

captions.F2: Examples of diverse task strategies generated by the same operator pool in VR simulation. In (a) spelling word blocks, (b) building a Jenga tower, and (c) setting up dominoes, operators used markedly different grasps and assembly sequences, yielding the behavioral diversity needed for pre-training.
captions.F3: The proposed policy architecture. Observations ($o$), past actions ($a$), image tokens, and noisy action chunks are processed in a single sequence. Causal sliding-window attention allows all chunks to be denoised in parallel during training, while rolling KV caching enables fast, asynchronous action prediction during inference.

sections.heading: Real-World Evaluation: Substantial Task Progress and High Reactivity
sections.summary: Across five challenging contact-rich tasks on physical hardware, the pre-trained model achieved significantly higher task success and progress than models trained from scratch. Conditioning on past history while replanning frequently with short action chunks (8 steps) maximized the benefits of pre-training.
sections.details:
Real-world evaluations tested unseen physical objects similar to those in simulation, fine-tuning policies with 1–2 hours of physical demonstrations per task. Five tasks were evaluated (Figure F4):
- (A) Plate racking: Lift a flat plate and insert it into a narrow slot on a drying rack.
- (B) Mug hanging: Pick up a mug with one hand, hand it over to the other hand, and hang it on a tree stand.
- (C) Jenga playing: Push a block out of the tower with one hand, pull it free with the other, and place it on top.
- (D) Cup stacking: Unstack nested cups and build a pyramid.
- (E) Bottles in bin: Grasp bottles on the table and toss them into a bin.

### 4.1 Effect of Pre-training
Across 20 evaluation trials per task, SPD consistently outperformed the from-scratch behavior cloning baseline in task progress. Looking at training loss curves (Flow Matching loss), which positively correlate with downstream task performance in imitation learning, SPD started with a lower loss and reached a substantially lower final convergence value. This shows that low-level contact primitives learned in simulation—such as fingertip pinching, scooping, and bimanual coordination—serve as strong initializations for real-world tasks.

### 4.2 History Conditioning and Action Chunk Length Ablation
The authors varied the sliding window size $w \in \{1, 32\}$ and action chunk size $c \in \{8, 32\}$. Conventional models (such as $\pi_0$) typically use no history ($w=1$) and output long chunks of about 1 second ($c=32$, ~1 sec at 30 Hz). However, when shortening the chunk to $c=8$ with $w=1$, the policy lost temporal consistency, causing the hands to jitter and performance to collapse.
In contrast, providing 32 steps of history ($w=32$) transformed behavior completely. Because past context guarantees temporal consistency, the policy can use short chunks ($c=8$) to react quickly to environment changes. The $w=32, c=8$ configuration achieved the best performance overall, boosting average task progress by 18 percentage points over training from scratch (whereas other settings improved by 3 points or less). In contact-intensive dexterous manipulation requiring continuous adjustments, conditioning on history and replanning rapidly is key to unlocking the full value of pre-training.

captions.F4: Autonomous real-robot evaluations across five tasks: (A) plate racking, (B) mug hanging with bimanual handover, (C) bimanual Jenga extraction and placement, (D) cup pyramid stacking, and (E) bottle binning. These tasks require precise coordination and high contact fidelity.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Horizons
sections.summary: This work proves that teleoperation data collected in physics simulation can serve as a powerful pre-training foundation for real-world multi-fingered hands. Future directions include expanding object diversity, mixing simulation with human videos and physical data, and using the policy to initialize reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
This study presented SPD, a framework for pre-training visuomotor policies for dexterous hands using VR teleoperation data collected in simulation. Combining 75 hours of simulation data with history-conditioned architecture enables complex physical bimanual dexterous manipulation with only minimal real-world fine-tuning.

### Limitations
- Dependence on physical parameter fidelity: Contact parameters such as friction and mass must be reasonably tuned so operators can execute realistic strategies. Data collected with unrealistic physics risks transferring poorly to physical hardware.
- Scene and object diversity: Pre-training was limited to 6 scenes, and physical evaluations used objects somewhat similar in geometry and characteristics to those in simulation. Generalization to entirely novel objects and environments requires further verification.

### Future Work
Simulation teleoperation is just one promising path for scaling data. A natural next step is building a hybrid pre-training corpus that blends simulation demonstrations with real teleoperation data and egocentric human hand videos. Additionally, leveraging the scalability of reinforcement learning (RL) without human time constraints by using this pre-trained policy as an exploration initialization is another promising direction.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details and Evaluation Rubric
sections.summary: The appendix details the VR infrastructure combining Quest 3 and MuJoCo, the real-world stack using Manus gloves and QP-based IK, and the scoring rubrics for each evaluation task.
sections.details:
The appendix covers system implementation details that ensure reproducibility.

- spd-vr implementation: MuJoCo runs on a host PC at 480 Hz and streams binary meshes to the Quest 3 via WebXR at 60 Hz. Operators use a 3-button foot pedal (checkpoint, pause, rewind) to control recording. Checkpoints cannot be created while objects are in contact, ensuring that rewinds always restart from a contact-free state.
- spd-teleop implementation: Inter-process communication uses ZeroMQ Pub/Sub to loosely decouple individual components into separate processes. Wrist tracking uses quadratic programming (QP)-based differential IK via mink, with interpolation applied to prevent sudden target jumps. For fingers, 25 keypoints captured by Manus gloves are calibrated per operator to drive the simulated hand model and compute 22-DoF joint angle commands.
- Real-world evaluation protocol: Each task uses a phased scoring rubric (e.g., in Jenga, partial credits are awarded for touching the block, pushing it 5 cm, extracting it, and placing it on top). Scores for each trial are normalized as a percentage of the maximum score, measuring fine-grained Task Progress rather than simple binary success/failure.

takeaways: Teleoperation data for fragile, expensive multi-fingered hands can be gathered in a VR simulator for pre-training without touching real hardware.
Contact primitives acquired in simulation transfer effectively to the real world with only 1–2 hours of additional physical demonstrations.

For contact-rich dexterous control, conditioning on observation history while replanning at high frequency with short action chunks (~0.25 s) achieves the best performance and maximizes pre-training benefits.
The simulation environment, VR collection software (spd-vr), and 75-hour dataset (spd-75h) are open-sourced, providing a strong platform for future dexterous hand research.
limitations: If simulated contact parameters like friction and mass diverge from reality, operators may learn unrealistic manipulation strategies that fail to transfer.
Pre-training was conducted in 6 scenes and tested on objects within similar categories; generalization to completely unseen environments and objects remains unproven.
VR teleoperation still demands human operator time, imposing labor cost bottlenecks compared to fully automated data generation like autonomous simulation RL.
